qualifications: The exact proof differs across software, consumer goods, and regulated products.
claims.statement: [[CustomerPull]] and [[ProductLedWillingnessToPay]] become durable only when distribution systems such as [[CPGDistribution]] can repeatedly deliver the product.

qualifications: Mission language without product performance or operating capacity is not sufficient.
claims.statement: A [[SaaSTrustMoat]] or [[PurposeDrivenBusiness]] can support adoption, but the trust survives only when operating pace and delivery remain credible.

qualifications: These sources do not establish one universally optimal portfolio or trading rule.
claims.statement: [[InvestmentRiskManagement]] and [[StopLossDiscipline]] treat uncertainty, position exposure, and exit rules as more reliable controls than confidence in one forecast.

qualifications: This is an analogical bridge from a late-Han political source into the business-and-markets topic; it should not be read as evidence about a modern commercial market by itself.
claims.statement: Hanji 1009 extends the topic's trust logic into talent access: [[ReputationConstrainedTalentProtection]] and [[TalentAttractionThroughRespect]] frame [[CaoCao]]'s decision to spare [[LiuBei]] as protection of future recruitment credibility.

summary: The business and market sources repeatedly separate attention from durable value: customer pull, distribution, operating capacity, trust, and disciplined risk management determine whether an attractive idea survives contact with real markets. Hanji 1009 adds a source-scoped political analogy in which Cao Cao's reputation for protecting a surrendered rival preserves future access to talent.
